c.tagline: Poland's regal heart of history and legend.

hood_landmark.Stare Miasto (Old Town): Rynek Główny main square with the Renaissance Cloth Hall (Sukiennice)
hood_landmark.Kazimierz: the Old Synagogue and Szeroka Street in the historic Jewish quarter
hood_landmark.Podgórze: Schindler's Factory museum near Ghetto Heroes Square
hood_landmark.Nowa Huta: Plac Centralny, the centerpiece of the socialist-realist planned district
hood_landmark.Kleparz: Stary Kleparz, Kraków's centuries-old open-air food market

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing in the Old Town/Main Square and on trams; taxi overcharging — use apps

hood_desc: Stare Miasto (Old Town) is the historic core around the Main Square, best for first-time visitors who want to walk to major sights, restaurants, and nightlife, though it is the priciest and most crowded part of the city.
Kazimierz is the former Jewish quarter turned bohemian district, ideal for travelers after atmospheric bars, vintage cafes, street food, and lively nightlife just a short walk from the Old Town.

Podgórze is a quieter riverside district across the Vistula rich in WWII history such as Schindler's Factory and the former ghetto, good for those wanting a laid-back, local feel and cool cafes away from the tourist crush.
Nowa Huta is a planned socialist-realist steel-town district on the city's edge, suited to curious travelers drawn to communist-era architecture and history rather than proximity to central sights.

Kleparz is a practical, unpretentious area just north of the Old Town around the main train station and market halls, appealing to budget-minded travelers who value transport links and everyday local life within easy walking distance of the center.

water.note: Tap water meets EU standards and is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: Buy KMK tickets from street/onboard machines (coins and cards) or the Jakdojade app; contactless bank-card tap-in is being rolled out on trams. A 20-minute ticket costs about 4 PLN (~$1) and a 24-hour ticket about 20 PLN (~$5).
transit.hours: Trams and buses run about 5am-11pm, with a reduced night network continuing through the early morning.

food.name: Zapiekanka
food.desc: Half a baguette baked with mushrooms and melted cheese, then finished with ketchup and whatever else you point at. Krakow's late-night food.

places.name: Endzior
places.note: The window locals queue at in the Okraglak rotunda; open until the small hours.

places.name: Okraglak stalls, Plac Nowy
places.note: The round former slaughterhouse ringed with zapiekanka hatches, each with its own loyalists.

places.name: Hala Targowa
places.note: Market hall better known for late-night grilled sausage, with zapiekanka counters alongside.

food.name: Obwarzanek krakowski
food.desc: A braided ring of dough, boiled then baked and scattered with salt, poppy or sesame seed. Protected by EU name and sold from blue street carts.

places.name: Rynek Glowny street carts
places.note: Dozens of blue-and-white carts around the main square; buy early, they go stale by afternoon.

places.name: Living Museum of the Obwarzanek
places.note: Hands-on workshop where you shape and bake your own ring, then eat it warm.

places.name: Hala Targowa
places.note: Bakery stalls sell them fresh from the morning ovens, cheaper than on the square.

food.name: Pierogi
food.desc: Half-moon dumplings stuffed with potato and curd cheese (ruskie), minced meat, or cabbage and mushroom, boiled or pan-fried in butter.

places.name: Przystanek Pierogarnia
places.note: Hand-pinched dumplings at several branches, one open around the clock in the Old Town.

places.name: Pierogarnia Krakowiacy
places.note: Long menu of savoury and sweet fillings; a dependable central choice.

places.name: Pierogi Mr Vincent
places.note: Small kitchen turning out inventive fillings beside the classics; expect a short wait.

food.name: Zurek
food.desc: Sour rye soup with white sausage and a halved boiled egg, often poured into a hollowed loaf of bread.

places.name: Miod Malina
places.note: Warm, rustic dining room doing polished versions of Polish classics; reserve at dinner.

places.name: Pod Wawelem
places.note: Big beer-hall portions of zurek, pork knuckle and dumplings by the river.

places.name: Bar Mleczny Pod Temida
places.note: Communist-era milk bar still serving soup for a couple of zloty at shared tables.

food.name: Maczanka krakowska
food.desc: Krakow's own sandwich: slow-braised pork neck with caraway, piled into a bun and dunked in its own gravy.

places.name: Andrus
places.note: Revived the old recipe; the bun comes properly soaked rather than dry.

places.name: Hala Targowa
places.note: Weekend market stalls sell maczanka alongside the famous grilled kielbasa.

places.name: Miod Malina
places.note: Sit-down version of the classic pork dish for those who want a table and a glass of wine.

food.name: Oscypek
food.desc: Smoked sheep's-milk cheese from the Tatra mountains, grilled until it squeaks and served with cranberry jam.

places.name: Rynek Glowny market stalls
places.note: Highlander stalls grill it to order on the main square, busiest around the Christmas market.

places.name: Plac Nowy
places.note: Cheese sellers set up beside the zapiekanka rotunda most mornings.

places.name: Hala Targowa
places.note: Buy whole smoked rounds from mountain producers to take away.

food.name: Polish vodka
food.desc: Rye and potato vodkas drunk ice-cold in shots, plus flavoured classics like bison-grass zubrowka and honey-spiced krupnik.

places.name: Wodka Cafe Bar
places.note: Cramped, cheerful bar with dozens of infusions poured by staff who explain each one.

places.name: Pijalnia Wodki i Piwa
places.note: Deliberately retro PRL-style bar; cheap shots, herring on the side, open very late.

places.name: Mercy Brown
places.note: Hidden speakeasy cellar for a slower, cocktail-led take on Polish spirits.

food.name: Kompot
food.desc: Homemade fruit drink of stewed apples, plums or cherries served barely sweetened, the standard soft drink of Polish milk bars.

places.name: Bar Mleczny Pod Temida
places.note: Jugs of kompot on the counter next to the soup, poured into glasses by the ladle.

places.name: Milkbar Tomasza
places.note: Modern take on the milk bar with good breakfasts and house kompot.

places.name: Bar Mleczny Gornik
places.note: No-frills canteen where kompot comes with a two-course lunch for pocket change.

landmarks: Wawel Castle
A commanding Renaissance royal castle perched above the Vistula River, the historic seat of Polish kings and a UNESCO World Heritage icon.
Wawel Cathedral
The coronation church of Polish monarchs, notable for its gilded Sigismund Chapel dome and eclectic mix of architectural styles.
Rynek Główny (Main Square)
The largest medieval town square in Europe, ringed by colorful townhouses, churches, and the historic Cloth Hall.
Cloth Hall (Sukiennice)
A grand Renaissance market hall running through the center of the Main Square, a centuries-old symbol of Kraków's trading history.
St. Mary's Basilica
A twin-towered Gothic brick church famous for its wooden Veit Stoss altarpiece and the hourly trumpet call played from its tower.
Kraków Barbican
A rare, well-preserved circular medieval fortification once guarding the city gates, its turreted brick walls a striking Gothic silhouette.
St. Florian's Gate
The last surviving medieval city gate, a Gothic tower marking the historic entrance to Kraków's Old Town along the Royal Route.
Kościuszko Mound
A grassy man-made hill built to honor national hero Tadeusz Kościuszko, offering panoramic views over Kraków and the surrounding countryside.
Wieliczka Salt Mine
A UNESCO-listed underground mine with entire chapels, statues, and chandeliers carved from rock salt, including the famed St. Kinga's Chapel.
Kazimierz (Jewish Quarter)
Kraków's historic Jewish district, filled with atmospheric synagogues, cobblestone streets, and lively cafes steeped in centuries of history.

train.note: International trains leave from Krakow Glowny, right under the Galeria Krakowska shopping centre a few minutes' walk from the old town. Genuine sleepers run overnight to Budapest and westward on the EuroNight Carpatia, which reaches Salzburg early in the morning (it leaves Salzburg at 20:30 the other way, combined with the Chopin for Warsaw); the Prague, Vienna and Berlin services are day trains. Booking for the Polish EuroNight sleepers normally opens about 90 days ahead rather than the usual six months, so they are worth watching for. For Ukraine there is no direct train from Krakow - take a train or coach to Przemysl and change to Ukrainian Railways for Lviv and Kyiv, allowing time for the border formalities.

intl.to: Prague, Vienna, Budapest, Berlin & across Europe

bus.note: Most international coaches use the Krakow MDA bus station, built into the same complex as Krakow Glowny train station, so changing between the two is a short indoor walk. RegioJet also runs useful coaches toward Przemysl for onward Ukraine connections, and FlixBus is usually the cheapest way to Prague or Budapest if you do not mind 7-9 hours on the road. Tickets are cheapest booked online in advance; all these routes are within the Schengen area except services heading east.

ferry.note: Krakow is well inland with no ferries of any kind; the nearest sea ports are Gdansk and Gdynia on the Baltic coast, several hours north by train.

half.name: Auschwitz-Birkenau
half.blurb: The sobering former concentration camp memorial and museum preserving the memory of Holocaust victims.

half.name: Zakopane
half.blurb: Poland's alpine capital, a wooden-chalet mountain resort beneath the Tatras with folk culture and hiking.

half.name: Morskie Oko, Tatra National Park
half.blurb: A breathtaking glacial mountain lake reached by a scenic walk through the highest Polish peaks.

half.name: Dunajec River Gorge
half.blurb: A scenic limestone gorge traditionally floated by wooden raft through the Pieniny Mountains near Slovakia.

half.name: Ojców National Park
half.blurb: Poland's smallest national park, full of limestone cliffs, caves and a fairytale clifftop castle.
